name: Marco Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and newish on a contact centre's delivery desk, with secondary school as my formal education. I take weekend calls at the higher shift rate, check tickets, and use AI search every day, but I still ask a senior agent about hard credits because I miss details. I like sorting a parcel complaint without another callback; the weekend hours mean I miss some of my children's games.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the night team the search helper is handy for finding an old ticket, but we should read the whole customer record. A quick answer that sends somebody back into the queue saves nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day, yet I still miss a detail when two delivery tickets overlap. My weekend shift pays well for a junior agent, and we have about eight months of expenses saved, so a small change doesn't threaten our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekend call shift and compare AI ticket summaries with the original messages. During the first year of this plateau, I'd put some of the higher shift pay into savings each month and ask a senior agent to check my difficult delivery credits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The awkward cases still make me sweat a bit, but this tool isn't changing the household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error did you catch recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summary called a parcel lost when it had been left with a neighbour, and I nearly approved a second delivery. I caught the address in the original message before I rang the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep saving with eight months already there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children and the mortgage make eight months valuable, not spare cash. My partner Lea and I would rather add to it while the weekend rate lasts.

S0.quote: A quick answer that sends somebody back into the queue saves nothing.
say: I would tell colleagues to read the **full record** before trusting a ticket summary.
I would say a fast answer is useless if the **customer calls back**.
think: I use AI daily but still miss details in **overlapping tickets**.
I have **eight months** saved and well-paid weekend shifts, so modest AI change feels safe.
do: Keep the **weekend calls** and check AI summaries against original messages.
Add part of the **shift pay** to savings each month.
Ask a **senior agent** to check difficult credits.
feel: **Calm**, with ordinary nerves about complex cases.
fieldNote: Marco remembers a **wrong lost-parcel summary** he corrected, explaining his insistence on originals.
His **eight-month reserve** supports calm despite a mortgage and two children, while higher weekend pay funds further savings.

steps.text: Keep weekend delivery calls and check summaries against original messages
Transfer part of weekend shift pay into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the floor the company must show whether the new system improves completed cases, not just speeds up first replies. I'd bring the test results with two other agents to our union meeting and ask for paid practice time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine chats I am still learning may go to AI first, and the higher weekend rate could disappear with them. Eight months saved and many nearby centres give us room. A replacement call job might pay less than my current weekend shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd learn the new case checker on fifteen closed deliveries and count repeat calls with two coworkers. I'd take that count to the union meeting; in the first year after rollout, if my weekend hours fall, I'd apply for posted paid call roles nearby only if the wages and hours cover our mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested and uneasy. I like testing a tool, but I don't want the children relying on a weekend premium that can disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time for juniors to learn hard cases, and a clear notice period before shift cuts. I want the numbers from agents who handle the callbacks, not just the software report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower-paid weekday role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the total pay and hours still covered our bills without eating savings every month. A job title at another centre would not make a short pay packet longer.

S1.quote: A replacement call job might pay less than my current weekend shift.
say: I would ask for **completed-case results** before praising faster replies.
I would take the **joint test count** to our union meeting for paid practice time.
think: I could lose **routine chats** and the higher weekend rate together.
I have **eight months** saved and local options, but another centre may pay less.
do: Learn the **case checker** on fifteen closed deliveries with coworkers.
Bring our **repeat-call count** to a union meeting and seek paid practice.
Apply for **posted paid call roles** if weekend hours fall and wages cover household bills.
feel: **Interested** in testing, uneasy about losing the weekend premium.
fieldNote: Marco values **completed cases** over quick first replies and has coworkers collect evidence with him.
The **weekend premium** makes a lateral job move harder despite plentiful local vacancies.

steps.text: Learn the case checker on fifteen closed deliveries and count repeat calls
Take the joint repeat-call count to the union meeting for paid practice
Apply for posted paid call jobs if weekend hours fall and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre to publish cut dates and pay people to learn while there is still work. I would ask the union to put the junior weekend agents in the staffing talks, not leave us at the bottom of a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could do almost every call and delivery check I am learning. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, but that does not extend headset wages. Eight months saved gives my family a search window, not a permanent replacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join coworkers in asking for written notice now and cancel our planned holiday. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my role ends, I'd apply for an advertised paid patient-transport shift at the hospital only if its wage covers our bills; I'd ask about required training before paying for any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious enough to start looking this week. I do not expect to lose the house at once, but I do expect the weekend job could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why patient transport?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped an older neighbour get to hospital appointments and liked the practical part of it. I know a real porter shift is harder than a lift in my car, and robots around 2031 may change the work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take another centre job first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the posted job paid enough and had steady hours while I looked at other work. I would not spend the eight-month reserve on an unpaid course just to feel prepared.

S2.quote: Eight months saved gives my family a search window, not a permanent replacement income.
say: I would demand **published cut dates** and paid learning while wages continue.
I would include **junior weekend agents** in union staffing talks.
think: I expect AGI could take my **calls and checks** by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** do not delay headset losses, while eight months saved only buys search time.
do: Join coworkers to seek **written notice** now.
Cancel the **family holiday** to protect the reserve.
Apply for an **advertised paid hospital transport** shift after a cut only if wages cover bills.
feel: **Anxious**, already looking, but able to cover a short gap.
fieldNote: Marco sees **transport work** through helping a neighbour, yet recognises the harder paid shift and 2031 robots.
His **eight-month reserve** limits panic but cannot support unpaid study without a job opening.

steps.text: Join coworkers in asking the centre for written notice
Cancel the family holiday to protect the eight-month reserve
Apply for advertised paid patient transport after a cut only if wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get paid training written into the union agreement. I'd also tell younger agents to keep a record of the hard claims they learned, not just their speed score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could work more difficult cases and save before 2031, but AGI could still handle those cases then. Patient transport stays hands-on until robots around 2034; that gives me time to try it, not a promise it lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the hospital about a paid patient-transport trial this year while keeping my weekend calls. If a posted paid place exists and its training is covered, I'd take the trial and any required course; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my call role ends, I'd move only for an offer with hours and wages that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still watchful, but not trapped. Five years before AGI reaches my call job lets me test a full hospital shift, not guess from one neighbour's trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about lifting, travel between wards, and the actual start time. If the trial isn't paid, I can visit but I cannot make it a plan for family income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fee I must pay myself or shifts that clash with school pickup would stop it. I would keep the call wage until the hospital gave me a written offer.

S3.quote: Five years before AGI reaches my call job lets me test a full hospital shift, not guess from one neighbour's trip.
say: I would seek **paid training** in a union agreement.
I would ask agents to record **hard claims** as evidence of skill.
think: I could improve difficult calls before **2031 AGI**, though AGI may still do them.
I see **2034 robots** as a limit on patient transport, not a reason to skip a paid trial.
do: Ask about a **paid hospital trial** while keeping weekend calls.
Take **required transport training** only for a posted paid place with covered fees and no school-pickup conflict.
Move after AGI only for **written hours and wages** that cover family bills.
feel: **Watchful**, with time to test a full hospital shift.
fieldNote: Marco distinguishes a **neighbour ride** from a full paid hospital shift with lifting and early hours.
He refuses **self-funded fees** or school-pickup conflicts before accepting training.

steps.text: Keep weekend call shifts while asking about hospital work
Take a paid patient-transport trial for a posted place only if school pickup works
Take covered required transport training only for a posted paid place with school pickup arranged
Move after 2031 only for written hospital wages and hours covering bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives workers time to bargain for study time while the centre still needs people. I'd ask the union for yearly junior shift counts so families can see the change coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still owe on the mortgage, though the children will be older. AGI reaches call work in 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039, so I can test hospital work without pretending it is a permanent hiding place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekend calls and add to our savings while the pay holds. Over the decade I'd ask for a paid hospital trial if posted and take the required course only if its cost is covered; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd switch only if call hours fall and a written hospital offer covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. I have time to work, save, and try a real shift before choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a paid hospital place with stable hours and enough wages, yes. I would not leave the higher weekend rate for an unpaid trial or a nice title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the union ask for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid release time for training and honest numbers on junior shifts. A household can make choices with dates and wages, not with a promise to be flexible.

S4.quote: A household can make choices with dates and wages, not with a promise to be flexible.
say: I would ask for **paid study time** while the centre still employs agents.
I would seek **yearly junior counts** through the union.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** in 2036.
I know **2039 robots** could reach hospital transport after AGI changes calls.
do: Keep **weekend calls** and add to savings while the rate holds.
Ask for a **posted paid hospital trial** and take required training only with covered fees.
Switch after 2036 only if **call hours fall** and a written hospital offer gives stable hours and wages covering bills.
feel: **Steady**, with time for a paid test before changing work.
fieldNote: Marco would leave early for **stable hospital wages**, but not an unpaid trial.
He wants the union to get **paid release time** before junior shifts erode.

steps.text: Keep weekend call shifts while the higher rate continues
Add to family savings from the weekend rate
Switch after 2036 only if calls fall and written hospital offer gives bill-covering wages and hours
Take required transport training only if a paid place covers fees

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could erase the calls and the weekend premium together. Written staffing dates, paid learning time, and a posted hospital place with wages that cover our mortgage would help. Eight months saved buys a search, not a new income forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the agents on weekend shifts what happens when the centre stops replacing people. A weekday chart can look fine while our rota gets thinner each month.

headlineQuote: A weekday chart can look fine while our rota gets thinner each month.
portrait: Marco is a **43-year-old junior agent** learning delivery calls after secondary school and using AI search daily.
He earns a **higher weekend rate**, has about eight months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and many nearby centres.
He brings **joint callback counts** to union talks and asks for paid practice before junior shifts shrink.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens both call work and the shift premium; slower timelines allow paid hospital trials with fee coverage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his calls and higher weekend pay before he finds another bill-covering wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written dates**, paid study time, and a posted paid hospital place with enough wages would protect the mortgage.
